utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I was located at Grebnice where we built bunkers and dug trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Continue.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I was in Zasavica where I performed the same type of work as in Grebnice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I was in Odzak. There, I did a number of jobs. First, I worked in the SUP headquarters. And I did all the jobs that were required of me to do. After that, in Odzak, we had to enter together with the soldiers from the homes of Muslims and Croats and bring out everything which they demanded that we bring out. After that, in Odzak, we entered Muslim and Croat homes where we would be loading coal and firewood. After that, I worked in Grebnice on a farm where I was given cleaning jobs. After that, I worked on the harvesting of wheat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In Obudovac. This same type of work I performed in Gornja Slatina. After that, I worked in Brvnik in building bunkers and digging cross-trenches. And the last job which I performed was the cleaning of a farm in Pisari, cleaning and other jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, my limited knowledge of geography I think suggests that Zasavica -- sorry, I'll start again. My limited knowledge of geography suggests that the silo is in Bosanski Samac. Is that right, in the town?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they are located in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zasavica is in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's in proximity of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What about Grebnice? Is that in the municipality of Bosanski Samac or where else?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obudovac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Also within the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Gornja Slatina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Also on the territory of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the last two, Brvnik and Pisari?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Also in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the first job you did, the silo job. What exactly did that involve?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: There, we were assigned. We were taken to the roof of the silos with sand bags, and it was there that we were building a type of a bunker, because the Serbian soldiers were setting up their machine-gun nests, and that is why we carried up the sandbags.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to carry up heavy sandbags, fairly heavy sandbags?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upstairs to the top of the silo?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we had to carry these bags, these sacks, up to the roof, to the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the machine-gun emplacement was at the top of the silo?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on top of the silo. It was on the top of the silo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Manned by Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were located there, on the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you guarded at this work site?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In performing this job, were you ever there when the machine-gun emplacement was firing or being fired upon?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: A couple of times it did happen that there was fire, machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you perform that work for?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately a few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who were the soldiers manning the machine-gun emplacement?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the 4th Detachment was?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever come along and inspect how the sandbag emplacements were going, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't come there. I didn't have the opportunity of seeing him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How long -- thank you. Do you know a place called Prud?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a small village very close to Bosanski Samac, is it not, across the Bosna River?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't mention it before when you were listing your work. But did you perform any labour at that site, at that place, or close to it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had an assignment there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in the sequence would you put it in relation to the silo job? Was it after the silo job or much later or what?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: After the silo job. It was then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber what the nature of the work was.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: There, we were building a bunker. And after that, we had to also do some work around a tank which was located there in the direction of Prud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the tank?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had to dig the embankment so that then the soldiers could place the tank at that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many workers were engaged along with you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately five or six people were working with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think I asked you were how many were working with you at the silo job. Can you just tell us how many were working with you there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I believe approximately ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's back to this Prud job that you were doing. In the time that you were working at Prud digging in the tank and digging bunkers, was there any exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was an exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far away were the enemy lines?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were rather close, and only -- the lines were very close because the only division was River Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, soldiers from which detachment or unit were active at this location at Prud?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you on this job in Prud doing the bunkers and digging in the tank?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately a few days, four to five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. What was the next job that you performed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Digging trenches and connecting trenches in Grebnice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Grebnice from Bosanski Samac approximately? I don't need to know precisely. Approximately.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I assume 5 to 6 kilometres. MR. Di FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many workers engaged on this particular job at Grebnice and what were their ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Some 15 to 20 people, all of us Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you engaged in trench digging at Grebnice?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this two months of continuous work there day after day, or did you occasionally have time off?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was we were working without interruption, day after day in Grebnice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this particular job, what time would your working start, what time would it finish?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: We would begin early in the morning at 7.00, 8.00 a.m., and end very late in the evening. The days used to be long, so we would be working 14, 15 hours a day, until 11.00 p.m., 12.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a summer job, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided with food?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell the Chamber how far away the enemy lines were? I use that word "enemy" just to differentiate between the people you were working for and the people who were engaged in warfare with them. So how far away from the enemy lines?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Depended. In some cases, the distance was between 50, 60 metres, up to half a kilometre or a kilometre, distance of a kilometre. It differed from place to place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described having performed work on occasions when there was exchange of machine-gun fire. Was there similar exchanges of fire at Grebnice while you were working?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the exchange of machine-gun fire, was there artillery and mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, while you were working?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, while we were working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did you have to do when you would dig a trench? Tell the Chamber how you would go about that task, what it involved. First of all, did you do it by hand, shovels, did you have earth-moving equipment? How did you carry out the job?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: All you received -- all we received were shovels and picks, and no earth-moving machinery, so it was all manual work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you started a trench, would you have to be working above ground, so to speak, because you hadn't yet dug yourself in?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you then be exposed to enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from digging, did you have to actually help construct the trench, put in ramparts, supporting beams and so on?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that heavy work, moving in those supports and beams and so on?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: It was very heavy work, because these were beams, railroad beams, sleepers, and they were very heavy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Mile Zoranovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he at Grebnice?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was guarding us in Grebnice while we were performing these jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Armed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was he attached to any particular unit?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you were working at Grebnice, were you ever required to clear vegetation to enhance the field of fire for the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, many a times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber what that involved.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in front of the bunker there was grass or trees. We had to clear that so that the visibility would be as good as possible. Everything had to be removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you often fired upon in these circumstances, or did the enemy hold their fire, perhaps knowing who you were?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were often fired upon because often the Serbs would open fire and provoke, and they intentionally provoked the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And fire would be returned?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was when you were clearing vegetation?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In effect, you would be placed in between the lines -- the enemy lines, so to speak, in front of the Serb lines and confronting you were the lines across the river, the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were working at Grebnice, was anyone wounded?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Fuad Bobic was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: He was wounded in the stomach and in his backside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what he was doing at the time, digging trenches, clearing vegetation, having his lunch? Have you got any idea?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: We were digging trenches at the time when the gunfire started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is he of what ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: After that, we had to carry him for about 2 kilometres to the building housing the command from where he was taken to the hospital. And don't know what became of him later. MR. Di FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P38, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps before you're shown that, can I just ask you one question. Were you ever paid at all, at all, for the work that you performed between April and December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never paid for those jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. MR. Di FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P38 now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document speaks for itself. You see over on the left-hand side of the document there's a number of names, and I think you'll see Mr. Bobic's name under the "injured." Do you see his name there, second on the list?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says he worked for 73 days, and that he was paid 10.950 dinars or rather there is an entry for 10.950 dinars next to his name. Were you aware of him ever being paid any money or given any money for his work?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to object at this time. The witness just testified that after the moment this person was shot and wounded he never saw him again. And then the question comes whether he was paid. How the witness can know that since he hasn't seen this person after this person was shot. Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: I'll tailor my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. Di FAZIO: I'll change my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until the time he was shot, was he ever paid?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of anyone else being paid a cent or dinar, anything at all? By that I mean your fellow workers between April and December 1992.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was ever paid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those months between April and December of 1992, were you short of money?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were short of money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those months between April and December 1992, as far as you're aware, were your fellow Muslims and Croats living in the town and municipality of Bosanski Samac short of money?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: They probably were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all the time that you worked, between April and December of 1992, was any record kept of the hours or the type of work that you did, other than, of course, for the sort of record that you see in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no record was ever kept of the hours people worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I should be a little more precise here. You weren't -- I'll withdraw that. Were you asked to keep a record of hours, days, and locations and types of work that you performed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never asked to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of your fellow workers at any time at all between April and December of 1992 recording details of hours or days or locations or types of work that they performed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw any of my work colleagues taking notes of their work hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any officials, such as, for example, Mr. Zoranovic, apparently record the days and the hours and the locations and the types of work that you performed? Did you ever see them writing down in their notebooks what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, he never took the notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I may come back to this document later, but I think for the time being, I've finished with it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the next job after Grebnice?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall precisely, but I believe it was the job in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do any work in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thinking back, which would you say you did first, Odzak or Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the sequence precisely. I can't tell whether Zasavica came before Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think I'd like to ask you first about Zasavica, so that's what I'd like you to direct your attention to, please. What sort of work were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: The same kind of jobs I did in Grebnice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I dug trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Clearing vegetation in front of the Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work there when there was fire being exchanged between the sides?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you guarded by armed guards?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were guarded by armed guards all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it was suggested to you that the guards were there for your protection, how would you react to such a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, they were not there to protect us. They were there to guard us and keep us from running away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that because in that period, many Muslims and Croats tried to escape, and many -- some succeeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any escape attempts at Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: While I was in Zasavica, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that in that period, many Muslims and Croats tried to escape and that some succeeded, are you referring to people who were engaged in this sort of work?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, what was the ethnic background of the inhabitants of Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly Croats, almost the entire village consisted of Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman named Dzevad Nukic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he work at Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April -- or rather in 1992, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was working at Zasavica, where was his father?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: He was working together with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to Dzevad Nurkic at Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an exchange of fire, and Dzevad Nurkic was hit in the head. 10, perhaps 15 minutes later, he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his father working there on the trenches as well?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His father was perhaps 50 metres away from Dzevad when this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he given an opportunity to watch his son die?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't -- unless there's an objection, I don't need to show you the document I showed you before. You can take it from me his name is mentioned there. And the document asserts that he worked for 32 days, and next to that, there's an entry for 4.800 Dinars. Are you aware of Dzevad Nurkic having been paid any money up until the time he was shot in the head?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't paid any money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Again, our friend from the Prosecution side is trying to create an impression which is really not appropriate. First of all, this document is dated 17th November, 1992. So obviously this amount of money cannot -- couldn't have been paid before to Dzevad -- the late Dzevad Nurkic only later to his family probably. But I don't really see what is the point of posing the question in this respect to this witness when from the same document which my learned colleague is referring to, we see that the document was created on the 17th of November, 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unless the Prosecution have the impression that a record could have been kept of the payment and then endorsed on that document? MR. Di FAZIO: With respect, I'm not of any impression if Your Honour please, and I don't see that you can draw the conclusion that Mr. Zecevic argues for from that the document. I see nothing in that document, nothing on the face of that document that suggests that there was a late payment. Nothing at all. The document says that it was created in November. It asserts that he worked for 32 days. It asserts next to that a sum of money. We don't even know if it was paid. For what it's worth, Mr. Zecevic may be perfectly right. He may be absolutely wrong. But there's nothing on the face of the document, nothing at all, that allows -- that leads you to the exclusion that he suggests you have to draw from looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: For that reason I think I'm perfectly entitled to ask if the man was paid for is work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think you can go ahead and ask that question, and Mr. Zecevic, this is a matter the Defence case can deal with when they call the evidence, as to whether or not any person listed on any document was actually paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour. I understand that. Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: Sorry, I don't recall if there was an answer to my question, but just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can ask the question again. MR. Di FAZIO: I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time, up until he was shot, did this boy ever receive -- this young man I should say, did he receive any money as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't paid any money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think you mentioned that you performed farm work at various locations. Can you tell us about that. First of all, can you list the locations at which you performed farm work. I'm not talking about going into people's houses; I'm not talking about trenches. I'm just talking about farm work now. First of all, where? Where did you do it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I did that in Pisari and at a farm in Grebnice. And after that, I worked twice, once in Obudovac, and once in Slatina harvesting wheat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't ask you in detail about each location. I just want you to give a general picture to the Chamber. First of all, what sort of jobs did you do at all of these locations? Just give us an idea of the sorts of work.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on those two farms, we had to clean, there was a lot of cattle there, cows. We had to clean out -- we had to clean the stables, to feed the cattle, to do all kinds of jobs that were needed on a farm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these privately owned farms or some sort of state enterprise before April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, before April 1992, those were state-owned farms, not private farms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were doing this farm work at these different locations, how would you get there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Every morning, we would come to the pensioners' hall and be picked up by a truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the same pattern apply? You would be driven to the location in the company of an armed guard, and were your fellow workers Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We would always go there accompanied by a guard, and the people were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the sort of sizes -- I'll withdraw that question. How many people would go to -- how many workers would go to these farms?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of hours did you work on these farms?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: That was not clearly defined. We could work for up to 10, 12, 15 hours. It all depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the shortest day that you ever worked, say would you say, when you were doing farm work?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: All days were the same. The hours were not defined, and I cannot remember the shortest day I spent doing such work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, perhaps we could find out if these farms were state-owned farms up until April of 1992, after April 1992, where was the ownership if they weren't state-owned any longer? MR. Di FAZIO: I don't need to repeat Her Honour's question. It's perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until April 1992, those were state-owned companies. Later, I don't know to whom they belonged. Perhaps they were in the hands of the military. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the running of the farm? Was it the same administration that was running the farm, same people working there running the place, making decisions, as had been there prior to April of 1992? If you don't know, say so. But if you can give us any information on that, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the same people remained there, the same people who worked there before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't actually exit or get out of Bosanski Samac until 1994. Do you know who was running the farms at that stage? If you don't know, just tell us. But if you've got any idea, tell us.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, those farms were run by persons of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presumably, when you went out to the farms, there was more than just the guard; there would have been other men, other workers, apart from yourself, your group of workers, who were doing things about the place. Did you have a chance to see them, see what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. While we were on a farm, we were alone with the soldiers. We, the people who were doing forced labour. MR. Di FAZIO: I don't think I can take the topic any further than that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever give consideration to escaping or trying to escape?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you didn't.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you didn't escape from this labour that you were performing because you didn't leave until 1994. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I left Bosanski Samac, that is, I got out, in December 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. What I'm talking about is the period of time in 1992 when you were performing this forced labour. During that time, you said that you gave consideration to trying to escape. I take it that you did not, in fact, escape.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't escape. But I often thought about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That brings me to my next question: What prevented you from making the attempt?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: What prevented me was the fact that my brother was in one of the camps, and I thought if I run away, there's no telling what might happen to him. They sometimes took their revenge on people who stayed behind. And that was one of the reasons why I didn't run away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons. If you had put your shovel down or whatever tool you were using on the farm and told the guard with the gun I'm sick of this, I want to go home, would you have been in a position to do that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you think the guard would have done in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. The objection is sustained. MR. Di FAZIO: I'll withdraw. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you were performing farm work, can you comment on the sort of food that was supplied to you, if any?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: We got soldiers' food, which was of very bad quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often were you fed? Once a day or twice or more often?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: It was one meal a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that usually?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Usually, thick bean soup or cabbage and bland. Very bad quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you hungry?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time December 1992 came around, had you lost weight?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how much?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: About 18 kilos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said your brother was in custody. When was he arrested?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, was he performing any of the sort of work that you've described?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He worked together with me at the silo. And we were also together at the bridge near the railroad where we did some digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you now to turn your attention to events in Odzak. Firstly, how would you be taken to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: With trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, was there an armed guard?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were going to Odzak, would women accompany you as well?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you receive the assignment to go to Odzak from in front of the pensioners' hall or were you directed there by some other means, directed to Odzak, I mean?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to rally there, report in front of the pensioners' hall. And it was there that we would receive the assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work in Odzak for?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately a few weeks, maybe a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct then that the system was you would assemble in the morning, you would be put on the truck, taken to Odzak where you would perform your work, and then trucked back to Bosanski Samac in the evening?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Women would accompany you back on the truck in the evenings?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of condition were they in when they would go back in the evenings, the women, I mean?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Very exhausted and tired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where would you be taken in Odzak upon arrival?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I was assigned to the SUP, the police station building. That is where they would take me, to their headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your job there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: All types of jobs. I had to bring in water, so I had to walk to a well some 500 metres away and bring in water and do all the other jobs they ordered me to do within the police headquarters building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you basically cleaning up the place and making it habitable after a recent conflict?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could state it in that -- put it in these terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Making it habitable and usable for whom? Who? Who would use that building, the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Who was using the building?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. As far as you're aware, while you were working there was anyone using the building, making use of it, for example --

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in use. It was used by the members of the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Were they engaged in fighting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of other work did you do in Odzak apart from carrying water and fixing the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: After that, we had to go into the Muslim and Croat homes and to bring out everything that they ordered us, all that was valuable. And we were to bring it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to get a bit more detail on this particular activity. Who would direct you to the particular houses?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be doing this job in groups of fellow workers?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were organised in the sense of being put into groups, organised in the sense of someone would take you and direct you to a particular house into where you would carry out this work?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about when you went into the house to get the material, get the property? Who would select what was to be taken?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers would select, those who were with us. So it was all that was of any value in that given home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the same men who told you which home to go into would be the man who told you what to select and take outside?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once a choice had been made as to what to take, would it be taken out?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened to the property?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: This property was then taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly it was taken away by these soldiers. They would be taking these items for their personal use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what soldiers they were? I mean it may be an obvious question, but I have to ask them sometimes. So what sort of soldiers were they?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, soldiers of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your role basically was just to empty the house, and after that, the stuff was taken away by others?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: My role was to bring the items out, to load them on a truck, and then they would be taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that you don't know actually know where the truck was taken, or you have through some information or other means you have an idea where the trucks were taken?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what was the destination of these trucks and where they are heading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you engaged in this sort of activity?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately a week or two weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of homes did you go into?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim and Croat homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to collect firewood and coal?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it customary in the countryside and towns and villages of Bosnia to collect coal and firewood during the summer for storage and eventually use in winter?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Customary, I take it, before the war?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- where did you go and collect the firewood and coal?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: We went into Muslim and Croat homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just want to establish a few other basic things first. Did you do so in groups, groups of workers?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we were performing this in groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your fellow workers Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive these assignments from in front of the pensioners' hall?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Doing these jobs, we did not receive orders for that in front of the pensioners' hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you directed to this particular type of job, namely, collecting firewood and coal?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, we were told to go to Odzak, and we only found out the type of job we would be doing when we arrived to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So -- right. Did you collect the firewood and coal only in Odzak or in surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In Odzak and the surrounding villages also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to go into homes to collect the firewood and coal?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of homes?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any idea of the ethnic background of the owners of the homes into which you went to collect coal and firewood?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Muslim and Croat homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the coal and firewood had been directed, what would be done with it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: The coal and firewood was taken to Bosanski Samac and to the surrounding villages and distributed to Serb families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, let's go into a little bit more in detail. Was it loaded on to trucks? Did you participate in that loading?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was loaded on to trucks, and I did participate in that loading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you accompany the trucks back to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it there distributed, as you say, to Serb families?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you help in unloading the trucks and delivering the coal and firewood?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did perform that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where exactly did you deliver the coal and firewood? Was it to private homes, or was it private homes and businesses or any other combination of destinations?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: We delivered to private houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time -- I'll withdraw that question. Just briefly answer these questions: In the time that you were mobilised after December, did you from time to time get relief from your fighting and go back home, back to your house, to rest up for a few days?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would get some leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you spent part of the winter of 1992/1993 in Bosanski Samac, or at least very close to it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that -- during that particular winter, I should say, were you supplied with coal and firewood to keep you warm?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who supplied it to you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: These were our stores from the earlier season. I didn't receive it from anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about during the winter of 1992/1993, did you have occasion to visit Muslim and Croat homes from time to time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have sufficient coal and firewood for their needs?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on whether the same conditions were being suffered by members of the ethnic Serbs in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you actually know that? Tell the Chamber what makes you say that. Is it something you saw or heard or what?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that people of ethnic ethnicity [as interpreted] were receiving coal and firewood for winter. Of Serb ethnicity. I saw people of Serb ethnicity receiving coal and firewood for the winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us about two episodes of trench digging that you were engaged in, Grebnice and Zasavica. Did you ever go back to trench digging in the period of time leading up to December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did return to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that particular location?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Brvnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far is that from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 10 to 12 kilometres. I don't know exactly, but I believe it's approximately that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned features in your testimony this afternoon of going to these work assignments, and groups of Croats and Muslims being guarded at these work locations. Did the same conditions apply in Brvnik?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the same in Brvnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also mentioned in your testimony that when you were engaged in other trench digging exercises, there was live fire going on between the two sides. Did the same apply to Brvnik?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you working in Brvnik?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately a few weeks, not very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And prior to your mobilisation, was the last job that you had at Pisari, and was that farm work?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of those features that I have been asking you about this afternoon, the guards, your fellow workers and their background and so on, did the same considerations apply to that particular job?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to turn -- ask you to turn your attention to other aspects of events in Bosanski Samac during 1992. Perhaps we could start off with this. MR. Di FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P40, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just have a quick look at that document. MR. Di FAZIO: For the benefit of Your Honours, this is the document referring to the prohibition of the gathering of three or more Muslims or Croats and signed by Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I think you'll see that it is dated August 1992, the 4th of August, 1992. It speaks for itself. You can see what it says. Were you aware of any prohibition or edict or order in existence prior to August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thinking back, can you recall when you first become aware of this prohibition against the gathering of three or more Muslims or Croats in public?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I heard for the first time about this over the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us any idea of when you heard this over the radio?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the month, but possibly two months after the takeover of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware -- I'll withdraw that. Other than the radio, was there any other source of information about this prohibition?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know about any other source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the months leading up to December of 1992, did you personally take care not to assemble in groups of more than three Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of other citizens of Muslim or Croat ethnicity taking the same precautions?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware, but probably they were undertaking -- adopting the same identical measure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the man who signed this particular document, Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no dispute that he was appointed the chief of police in Bosanski Samac. Did you ever see him in that capacity, speak to him, as chief of police?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I did have the opportunity of seeing him, but not of talking to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any writing of any form referring to such a prohibition, the prohibition we have just been talking about? I'm not talking about the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, such orders were posted in the city. You could see them in the city pasted on walls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Posters, I take it, were fixed around the town?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel to see that sort of order being posted around the town in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: I've finished with that document. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that your brother was arrested, and I think you gave us a date, the 5th of May. Can you tell the Court the circumstances under which he was arrested. What happened on the occasion that he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, 1992, members of the Serbian army entered our home with a paper which was supposedly a warrant to take my brother for an informative talk to the SUP. However, that after this interview he would be returning home, which wasn't what happened, because he didn't return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than informing you of the reason -- I'll withdraw that question and rephrase it. Other than telling you that they wanted to have an informative talk, did they provide any other reason for his arrest?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were just saying that they would be taking him in for an informative interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the men who arrested him locals or were they from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, both locals and two persons from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they appear to be policemen or soldiers, or couldn't you tell the difference?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: They all wore camouflage uniforms, and I couldn't tell the difference whether they were policemen or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of them?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Dragan Tugonjic, nicknamed Tugonja, and he was from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in any organisation, for example, police, or the 4th Detachment, or something else? If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again? I don't mean years later, but in the ensuing months.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him in the ensuing months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately four or five times in the ensuing months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In the street in front of the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the street?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: He was on two or three occasions standing in the street in front of the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not an objection but a question. What is the reason for this line of questioning? What is the reason for all these details? I think maybe our friend can explain that and maybe to stick to the indictment and to the general issues and important issues. I don't see that this kind of questioning is in accordance with the standard principle of proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is nothing wrong with this questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was my impression. Maybe I'm wrong. Sorry. MR. Di FAZIO: I'm happy to answer, that but it's 5.45. Perhaps the witness can be led out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We shall have a break and continue our proceedings at 18.05. We'll take 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, continue. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, this relates to your line of questioning. Page 74, line 6, where the name of this person is mentioned, it simply says "Dragan, Bosanski Samac." MR. Di FAZIO: I'm sorry, what page is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: 74, line number 6. So presumably the man's surname is missing, because I doubt his surname is the name of the town. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, I see the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just have the name of the man you recall who came along to arrest your brother, one of the men anyway. We got the first name in the transcript, that's Dragan. But what about the surname?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Tugonjic, T-u-g-o-n-j-i-c, nicknamed, Tugonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, what I'm actually interested in when I ask you about visits to your brother is whether or not you saw at the SUP or in the vicinity of the SUP any of the defendants during those visits.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I visited my brother only once, but I saw Mr. Simo Zaric a couple of times. On one of those occasions, he was entering the building of the SUP. MR. Di FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment while I check something in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier before the break that you saw your brother about four or five times in the ensuing months following his arrest and now you say you saw him once. Either I misunderstood your earlier answer or there's been some other problem. What is your position? Following his arrest, how often did you see your brother?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that the occasion that I saw Mr. Zaric going into the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the defendants on other occasions in or near the vicinity of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in the vicinity of the SUP, but I saw Mr. Tadic a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the one occasion that I saw your brother, what sort of physical shape was he in?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In very bad shape. He was covered with bruises, and he had lost a lot of weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any blood on him?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your mother permitted to visit him more often?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but those were not regular visits. You just brought some food and water and tried to get them through while staying outside in the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the occasion you saw your brother, did you try to get food and supplies to him?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you successful?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you went to visit your brother only once in that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that time, I was under work obligation. And the second reason was that I was afraid I might be arrested, too, if I happened to be in the vicinity of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want you to turn your attention to June and July of 1992. Was there ever an occasion when men came to your home demanding money and jewellery and so on?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the men who came to your home and how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: That happened twice. The first time was in April when two members of paramilitary units from Serbia came to my house and brought Hasan Bicic with them. They demand from me, my brother, and my parents to gather the amount of 1.000 deutschmark within 15 to 30 minutes. And they said if we managed to do that, they would release Hasan Bicic. My brother tried to put that amount together within the given time, which was impossible, because there was no one who could give you that sort of money. And when my brother returned empty-handed, they left, taking my brother's car with them. And they also took two gold chains off my neck, and they left, taking Hasan with them. The second time was in June --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before we get on to June, and thank you for raising the incident with Hasan Bicic. I'll get on to the June incident in just a moment, but there's a couple of matters I want to clarify from this April incident. First of all, what sort of condition was Hasan Bicic in?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Hasan Bicic was in very bad state. He had a broken nose. He had many scars on his face. He was black and blue and covered with blood. He had blood stains on the clothes he was wearing. He was very thin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men you say were from Serbia. Were they dressed in paramilitary-type uniform, camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms; but on their sleeves, they had the emblem of the Grey Wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What happened to your brother's car? Did you ever see that again?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you feel that you could do anything to get the car back? Did you feel, for example, you could go to the authorities or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't even think about it. I knew it was futile. I knew that we would never see the car again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can I ask you to tell the Chamber of the event in June that you started to describe.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In June, members of the paramilitary formations from Serbia, Seselj's men, came to our house. There were three of them. At the time, my parents and my neighbour, with his wife, were in our house. They started searching our house and demanded from me and my mother to hand over all the jewellery and money that we had. On that occasion, my father, my neighbour, and I were mistreated. They beat us the whole time. Throughout the time they were there, they threatened me and kept telling my mother that they would kill me. The one who introduced himself as their commander demanded from me that I address him as "Mr. Chetnik." And all the time he held a pistol and a knife in his hands and kept putting the gun to my temple and the knife to my throat and asked my mother: "How do you want us to kill him? Do you want us to shoot him in the head or slit his throat? I think it would be quicker to slit his throat. It takes only two seconds. It would be better." And all that time, he kept shooting around the room at the ceiling. And once a bullet was fired between my legs and hit the couch. He also gave me a piece of paper and told me to write a list of all the members of the SDA and the HDZ, which, of course, I didn't do because I didn't know all the members of these two parties. After that, he brought a bottle of whiskey, put it in front of me, and told me to drink. And I had to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to drink the whole bottle?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was summer. There was no water or electricity at the time. And my mother put the fire stove on to cook lunch, and it was terribly hot in the room. I don't know how much I had drunk before I passed out. And I simply don't know what happened after that. Later, when I came round, they told me they would return in half an hour, and that the list should be ready by then. Otherwise, they would take me with them. After that, I lost consciousness again and woke up in my aunt's house. And on that occasion, a certain amount of money was taken away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was damage caused to your family's possessions in the house?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was broken or damaged?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they kept firing all the time that they were there. All the windows were shattered. They fired into the ceiling making many holes. And just before leaving, the one who asked me to call him Mr. Chetnik took the knife out and made -- and broke the television set and other pieces of furniture. They turned the house upside down trashing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Had you ever seen these men before in Bosanski Samac or did you see them subsequently in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I had never seen them in town before. I did see them later, though. But after that incident, I didn't see them again. It seems that they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hang on. That's not very clear. You say: I did see them later, though, but after the incident, I didn't see them again. What I want to know is following the episode where they shot around the house and forced you to drink liquor, did you see them around the town again on another occasion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them in town once, but not after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they in company with?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: They were in the company of strange people. I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were your father and brother eventually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the date when they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: The 5th November, 1992. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I want to produce a document that hasn't been produced before. It's an exchange list. It is material that was provided to the Defence as part of the Prosecution exhibits, so they have had it for a long, long time. And they have also been given copies today. Unfortunately, I don't have a translation at this stage. I didn't think -- anticipate that I would be needing it, but it just confirms one aspect of this witness's evidence. I am told by the case manager that if it's admitted, at least marked for identification today, we can have the full translation by the time we resume proceedings on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead. MR. Di FAZIO: Furthermore, the copy is not particularly clear, but I think it's sufficient for my purposes. I understand that Mr. Lukic may well have used the document in any event himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Witness, would you please look at this document that I produced to you. Witness, have a good look at it. Regrettably, it's not very clear. MR. Di FAZIO: If I may interrupt my questioning, I understand that Mr. Lukic may well have a better copy in his possession and that he may be able to assist the Court at a later stage. I don't think he has it here, but I understand he may be able to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as this document is concerned, I'm not sure I have a better copy. But regarding this list of people, there is another document for the same exchange, and that is a list made by the committee for exchange itself. I think it is much more legible, and I think I have an English translation as well. But the problem is I don't keep this document in my office in The Hague, and I will be able to provide this other document only at our next trial date, at our next hearing. Just one more clarification: Those are actually the same two documents. This particular list was made by the Red Cross, and another list of the same people was made by the commission handling the exchange. And this other paper is much more legible. MR. Di FAZIO: When the time comes, if that other document is tendered or produced by the Defence, I'm sure that will assist us in reading this particular document. In the meantime, can I proceed with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number for identification only, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's P52 ter ID. Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, all I want you to do is quickly have a look at the document, and it is beyond dispute that there are a number of names there. Have a look at number 11 there -- doing the best you can, can you read the name there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Esad Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your brother's name?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And doing the best you can again, go to item number 46 on the list. Doing the best you can, can you read the name there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Sabrija Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the purposes of the transcript, would you please read the heading of the document. That is the writing at the top of the list in the middle of the page and I think it starts with the word "Komisier".

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: "Committee for the exchange of arrested and other persons." And then again, it says: "For exchange on the 5th of November, 1992" writes down - I'm not sure about this word - "the following persons." MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you very much. I've finished with the document. And if Your Honours please, I will have a full translation, I hope, by the time we resume in May at stage I will be seeking to have it tendered fully into evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to November 1992, had your family been making attempts to engineer or bring about an exchange for yourselves?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we tried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber of your efforts to get exchanged. Where did you go? How often did you go there? What did you do when you got there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Every time we heard there was an exchange coming, my mother went there to see if she could be included. However, she was not successful until that very date when she was actually exchanged. And my father did the same thing. He tried to put his own name on such a list for exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever accompany them when they went to wherever it was to attempt to get on a list?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the location of the place? Where did you go in order to try and get on this list?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the headquarters of this commission for exchange was in the building -- in the headquarters of the social welfare building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the defendants present?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to him in connection with getting exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I did speak to him about an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber what you said to him as best you can recall, and what he said to you, as best you can recall.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked Mr. Tadic whether he could place us on the list for the exchange, and Mr. Tadic gave an affirmative answer. However, this exchange which took place on the 24th of December, 1992, I was on the list in front of my mother. But the next day when the exchange was to take place, I wasn't on the list any more. Instead of my name, there was another name entered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to see any lists and see your name on any list? Where did you see such lists and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In the building of the social welfare where the commission for exchange had its headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the lists put up on a wall or something?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. The list was in an office. That was the deputy of Mr. Tadic where I could see -- he showed me the list and I could see my name and the name of my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P52, the document ter ID, the document I just showed you, indicates that the exchange was on 5th of November, 1992. Can I take it that you saw some sort of list on the day before, the 4th of November?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question, whether I've seen the list before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry if I've misled you. Let me start again. When did you first see your name on any list for exchange?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it on the 23rd of December, the day before the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your mother was exchanged when?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to know how it was that you came to see your name on the list on the 23rd of December. Did you go to the office specifically?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone show you the list?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you examine the list?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw your name and your mother's name?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following day, the 24th, was the day of your mother's exchange. But you were not exchanged. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following day again, did you have a chance to examine any list?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
