utterances.text: How do you know your name was taken off the list?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Because prior to the exchange when people are going on the -- boarding the buses, the names on the list are read out. And prior to my mother's name, another name was read out, and I wasn't on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I assume you and your mother went along ready to be exchanged, but she was the lucky one and you weren't. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So now you found yourself in a situation where your whole family had been exchanged, your brother and father had gone the month before, and your mother went on the 24th, and now you were left in Bosanski Samac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What did your family members take with them when they were exchanged? I don't want every item, but were they able to take large items, or did they just have a bag or something?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: They could take just a few personal items, not very many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain living in the family home?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now turn your attention to another issue, please. Are you familiar with a place called the Spomen Dom?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that place?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In the memorial hall, before the war, it was the headquarters of the radio station with a few shops and a few conference venues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, did you ever go to any meetings there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, the members of the 4th Detachment called upon all Muslims and Croats to come and report to the memorial hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they go about calling upon all Muslims and Croats? Was it a radio announcement, a letter, personal visit? How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Was it -- it was either the radio or in written form; however, we were all told to come and report there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any of the defendants there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he participate actively in the meeting in the sense of speaking or doing anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He held a speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the effect or the thrust of the speech?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, essentially, they gathered us in order to mobilise us and to give us rifles. And the speech of Mr. Zaric was -- went in that direction. If we would take up weapons, we would have certain privileges, and we would be relieved of our work duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the word that he used to describe work duty?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot -- I cannot remember exactly. Did he mention work duty or forced labour? I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When he referred to work duty, did you understand that to be a reference to the sort of things that you had been engaged in during the preceding months?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the meeting take?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 40 minutes, up to an hour. Not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the -- withdraw that question. What ethnic background were the assembled men?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst them, did you recognise any men who had been engaged in work details and work assignments, or forced labour, of the sort that you had been doing?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the men take up the offer?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following that meeting, did any of the men who had been assembled leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that take place?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that on the very same night or the next night, a big group of Croats and Muslims left -- fled, and swam across the Sava River to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following that episode of the men swimming across the Sava to Croatia, were there any arrests of women and children, or rounding up of women and children?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, yes. All those people who swam across the Sava River, their families, mothers, fathers, wives, children, they were all arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see any of this process occurring with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see when my neighbour and her two sons were taken in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to seeing your neighbour and her two sons being rounded up, did you come to hear of the people who had been rounded up having been taken to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear it. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's 12 minutes to 7.00. I've got only a brief matter that I need to raise, but I'm informed by Defence counsel that they had another matter they wanted to raise. I was told some 15 minutes before closing today's session. I don't know if that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: So I don't know if this would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will adjourn the proceedings until the 1st of May at 14.15 hours. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, it's precisely that I want to now raise with the Chamber. In fact, I suppose it concerns this witness as well. I understand, I wasn't here the other day, I read the transcript, I understand we're resuming on the 1st of May, which is a Wednesday, and that the Chamber has granted the Friday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, for the religious observation of the defendants. MR. Di FAZIO: That's right. That means that we will have two days of sitting that week, Wednesday and Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: I haven't got too much more to go with this witness, probably about another hour I would say. And then there's cross-examination. We no longer have any witnesses I'll say locally, that is, close to The Hague who can be slotted in quickly. I wonder if the Defence could indicate how long they will be in cross-examination when we resume in May, because we could face a situation, for example, where I take a part of Wednesday, and cross-examination starts on Wednesday and continues on Thursday, and then we finish there and then, and then we will be breaking for three days. If we have got a witness from Bosnia that means they have to sit around in a hotel room for three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I can find out from the Defence. MR. Di FAZIO: If we have some idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are saying you need an hour more to complete examination-in-chief? MR. Di FAZIO: About an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. MR. Di FAZIO: What I'm concerned about is bringing in someone for half an hour or an hour's testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then hold them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was wondering if the Chamber was minded to adjourn early on Thursday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think I can find out just roughly because you haven't yet finished so they wouldn't know what the other one hour would reveal. Anyway, just roughly, if they have a statement. Yes, while the Defence -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours. I have been informed that my colleagues will take four hours, I will take one hour, and Mr. Pantelic informed me half an hour. So all in all, five and a half hours. Of course, subject to whatever the witness is going to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have a question to the Prosecutor, Mr. Di Fazio. If my memory serves me right, you asked earlier during the witness giving his testimony whether during the first period of digging trenches, he received any food during work time. And if I am correct, the answer was no. Is that so? MR. Di FAZIO: Do you want me to clarify that particular issue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes. During that first period, and also the following periods of digging trenches, were they fed during work time? MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, I can clarify that now. I'll do that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cast your mind back to Grebnice, Zasavica, Brvnik, the places where you engaged in trench digging. Now, was it the case that in those places you weren't fed or provided with any food at all? Or was it just in the one location, or was there no established practice? Can you please clarify the situation for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: In Grebnice, in Zasavica, we received no food. But you see, the food, if we had something from one's home, we took it along. But we didn't get anything from the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that lack of supply of food from the soldiers the same wherever you went digging trenches? Or was it irregular? Sometimes you were provided, sometimes you weren't?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't receive food. They didn't give us food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a constant. They never gave you food at any of the digging locations. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't give us food. We didn't receive food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when trench digging, any food that you consumed during the day was stuff that you supplied yourself?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Maybe the witness can be taken out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, my case manager has kindly done the calculations on the estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: If we were to stick to our predictions, if that were to come true, we would finish about 3.45 on the Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: Sorry. 5.15 on the Thursday. 5.15 on the Thursday. So we would lose that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That bit of time. In terms of expense, it would definitely cost the Tribunal more to keep the witness over the three days. MR. Di FAZIO: Exactly. With respect, it's not just a question of expense, is it, Your Honour? They are from far away. In a strange environment. Three days -- it's strain on people and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, we will simply deal with this witness over these two days. Yes. The Trial Chamber was expecting Mr. Christian Rohde to come into the courtroom. I'm wondering if he may be somewhere outside, if the usher can check. Yes. The Trial Chamber wanted information on the facilities available to Mr. Milan Simic while he is in the detention unit during the proceedings. He has been signing his consent to be excused from attendance in the courtroom and the Trial Chamber is under -- has been given information that the videolink is working and that he is able to follow the proceedings. So the Trial Chamber wanted information from Mr. Christian Rohde especially regarding the mode of contact with his counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: May I approach a microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is one just in front of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to our research and time logs, the videolink is working well with an occasion hiccup so to say. It's not, let's say, a very simple tool. The videolink functions during the entire procedure while Mr. Simic is absent. The contacts with his Defence counsel, according to our time log, with occasional hiccups function well. The normal procedure is that Mr. Simic contacts a guard and is then able to use a telephone with, according to our calculations, with a delay in between 30 seconds and a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. And that is the position up to today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. We will hear from Mr. Zecevic what his instructions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would, Your Honours, if I may, I would like to introduce -- I would like to address this issue in Serbian language for the benefit of my client, because he is listening to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, if you can go slowly so that the interpreters can follow. I want to make it clear, that this is not an inquiry by the Trial Chamber. It will just be a question of you stating what you know from the instructions from your client, and that will be the end. Thereafter, the Trial Chamber will decide to do what -- if there is any need for any decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours. It will take just two minutes. I would like to explain just explain what is our position, the position of myself and my client. If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] As you are aware, Milan Simic and his Defence team have agreed with the arrangement introducing videolink into his cell in the Detention Unit. At any rate, that arrangement is not easy on our Defence or our client, because it involves certain problems. However, we appreciate that this trial needs to take its course unhindered. And in the interest of my client's health who, as you know, is a paraplegic with a high degree of disability, we have agreed that this trial proceeds with him remaining in his cell for most of the time following the course of the proceedings through videolink. On the other hand, this also implies that between the Defence team and the client, there is unhindered prompt and efficient communication. May I remind you that the Registrar has addressed us with two proposals, one of them being a laptop computer with a direct link, and the second alternative was a telephone line wherein I would pick up the receiver and immediately be able to speak to my client. And of course, he would be able to contact me that way as well. As far as the Defence is concerned, we have found this arrangement satisfactory until now because it gave us the opportunity to speak to our client with a delay of 40 to 60 seconds from the moment I would pick up the receiver. The day before yesterday, while visiting my client, I was allowed to visit him in his cell because of his condition. And in the course of our conversation, I asked him about his opinion on the way the arrangement was functioning. On that occasion, my client informed me that every time he wanted to speak to me while the proceedings were ongoing, he would press a button, which I assume is some sort of alarm button, or rather a signal going to the room of the guards on the ground floor, and then the guards would inform a third person in the administration of the Detention Unit - I believe his name is Harry - located on the same floor as my client, and after that the telephone set would be brought to my client physically. And only then is he able to speak to me. And when I ask him how long this procedure usually takes, he told me it was over ten minutes. And he doesn't think that this arrangement is really satisfactory from his point of view. I addressed the Registrar, Madam Registrar from the courtroom, and I explained the problem to her and asked her if we could find a solution to this problem, which I believe is of purely technical nature, without encumbering the Trial Chamber with it. However, two days later, I was informed that the problem cannot be solved without the assistance of the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber finds that their assistance is in order. And just one more thing, and then I'll conclude. Today, during our hearing, I had occasion to test this arrangement in practice. Namely, I will remind you of the moment when I made an objection regarding Document P38. According to the Livenote, which also makes a record of the time, the objection was raised precisely at 17.30. Our exchange of arguments and the decision of the Trial Chamber lasted until exactly 17 hours 02 minutes, 46 seconds. At 17.06.36, I was informed by the Registry that my client wished to speak to me. I answered the telephone, and my client told me that he had wanted to give me a clarification and an instruction regarding this particular document, and that he had asked to talk to me at the very moment when I was making the objection. In other words, it took him about five minutes to establish communication with me in order to give me a certain instruction. In situations like this, as well as situations of cross-examination, I believe that a five-minute delay is extremely long. And from that point of view, for that reason, I would kindly ask -- request on my client's behalf and in my own name that my client be enabled during the course of the proceedings to have a telephone set right next to him within his reach and to use it solely for the purpose of communicating with my telephone set so that we are able to exchange consultations or instructions within the shortest possible time. [In English] Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Any other matters to be raised by the Prosecution, the Defence? The Trial Chamber has two points: We have observed that during examination-in-chief, especially of the first witness this week, there was an amount of repetition of questions to the witness. And this does take time, because there's no need for repetition. And this was both on the Prosecution side and the Defence side when cross-examining. I do hope that the parties will take this into consideration for the next witnesses and avoid repetition of questions. The other point I wanted to ask the Prosecution is that before we resumed the proceedings the last time we adjourned, I had asked the Prosecution to consider recording some of the witness evidence under the provisions of Rule 92 bis. The Trial Chamber has observed that there appears to be no movements, at least we haven't seen any copy of any applications to the Registrar to move the matter into process. So I wanted to find from the Prosecution what the position is. The reason for our request really is to cut down on hearing time. We have observed that some of the witnesses spend a few minutes discussing the involvement of the accused, and under Rule 92 bis, most of the rest of the evidence can be placed in a statement and produced before the Trial Chamber. And then the rest of the evidence regarding the involvement of the accused and the other matters accepted under Rule 92 bis can be given viva voce. So I wanted to find out what the position of the Prosecution is in this, trying to work out Rule 92 bis to cut down on hearing time, what their position is. MR. Di FAZIO: Well, the position is that the Prosecution is aware that most of the remaining witnesses from now on will give evidence that at some point or another will touch upon the activities of the defendants themselves. And so for that reason, we thought that it best that they give their evidence orally, completely. If the Chamber, however, wants us to approach those witnesses who did speak about the defendants only from time to time in their evidence and put in the rest of their evidence pursuant to statements, then without committing myself, it's something that I'll immediately raise with the rest of the trial team and try to address. It may be that some witnesses would be quite -- their testimony would lend itself to using that system, and it may be that others would not be -- the nature of their testimony would not be such that we would prefer to have all of their evidence to be heard orally. I haven't made any moves to attempt to get any of the remaining evidence in under 92 bis because of the fact that they did touch upon the personal activities of the defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you notice, what we have observed, the evidence so far involves discussion about their arrest, first of all, the disturbances before 17th April, and then the arrest of some of the witnesses, the way -- the detention, the beatings, and then the work obligations in different places at different times. Most of that is on record with most of the Prosecution evidence. So that if the rest of the witnesses are also people who went through the same experiences as these other witnesses, it is possible to get most of that evidence on a statement, and only leave out the activities of the accused. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which can be given -- that evidence can be given viva voce in which case whether a statement under 92 bis is recorded or not, all the Prosecution witnesses may have to come and appear, especially for cross-examination. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But at least that would cut down the hearing time. In most cases, I think, to an hour in evidence in chief. Because it would be just the identification of the accused, how many times they saw whatever they were doing, and that can be put into mostly one hour if most of the other evidence is on paper, and then clarification here and there perhaps, and then cross-examination and then re-examination. It would cut down on most of the time. MR. Di FAZIO: It would. I've got no -- I don't take any issue over that. That's absolutely true. It would there's no question about that. I think that the Prosecution can conduct a review of the remaining witnesses and come up with some sort of list of witnesses who might, who could, give their evidence partially pursuant to the provisions of Rule 92 bis and partly orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: But I haven't conducted that exercise as yet principally because all of the remaining witnesses or the vast majority of them speak about some of these defendants. I can now, if the Chamber wishes me to, conduct such an exercise in conjunction with my colleagues and do that. Does the Chamber wish me to embark to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber would urge the Prosecution to do that. It's an exercise that is possible. And like I say, you can divide the evidence. Touching the defendants, you leave that out, the rest of the evidence comes on paper, and then when the witness is in Court, you fill up what is remaining, and then the cross-examination can be conducted. In fact, even if all the witnesses except for the three experts were allowed to give most of the evidence in written form, they would still have to come for purposes of cross-examination and also filling in the activities of the accused for those who have anything to say about that. But I'm sure that it would cut down the time, almost one-third of the remaining time that we have. MR. Di FAZIO: It would be a big drain, though, on the resources of the Prosecution. We would have to -- I haven't got the rule right in front of me as I am speaking to you, but I think it would require --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It does require appointing a presiding officer. MR. Di FAZIO: Appointing a presiding officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the presiding officer travelling to the venue, wherever it is. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, exactly. And obviously trial team -- members of the Prosecution team would have to go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the members of the team to make sure that the statements are properly -- MR. Di FAZIO: Pertains to what the Prosecution wants, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The idea of Rule 92 bis is really to cut down on hearing time, because the Tribunal, as you know, is loaded with pending trials. And we are very concerned about accused persons waiting for too long. MR. Di FAZIO: Very well. Can I say this, then: The Prosecution will conduct an exercise of review of the remaining witnesses and endeavour to come up with perhaps a list of witnesses who would be suitable, we think, to adopting that procedure in respect of those particular witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: And I can report to you when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because the Trial Chamber is aware that the nature of the evidence will not change. Because instead of the brief statements given to the Defence, it will be a full statement in each case, in which case it will even be better for the Defence. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I understand what Your Honours are saying completely. And as I said, I'll undertake this review and to -- and report to you when we resume again. And I'm sure that we can make some headway adopting this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. Di FAZIO: I'll do my best efforts to make sure we utilize the procedure. Some of the witnesses will talk about issues that don't concern these defendants or don't touch upon the activities of these defendants directly. For example, some witnesses will talk about the Crkvina massacre, the site where quite a large number of people were murdered, in Crkvina, a small village close to Bosanski Samac. That sort of evidence, for instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think it's premature to speak about the -- in terms of massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, will you sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Nobody is giving evidence. Mr. Di Fazio is not giving evidence. MR. Di FAZIO: Now, that sort of thing would be the first time the Chamber will be hearing about it, and that sort of evidence I would like to present orally in Court. But nonetheless, I know what Your Honours are saying about many witnesses going over the same sort of phenomenon that we've heard about, the arrests, the torture, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look at the provision of Rule 92 bis, it is not necessarily only that aspect that it is the same type of evidence. If it would be completely new, I realise as long as it isn't on the activities of the defendants, it can be put in a statement. MR. Di FAZIO: It can. All I was saying is that there are some types of topics, some sorts of topics that, as a Prosecutor, I would want you to hear about firsthand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that has always been a problem in lots of trials because the Prosecution usually would prefer to have evidence heard by the witnesses and all and sundry, that is understood. But the Trial Chamber's view is that even that can be put in a statement. After all, it would be public, it would be in the public records. MR. Di FAZIO: I'll conduct that exercise, and I'll report to you when we receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. Di FAZIO: The use of 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall now adjourn until the 1st of May at 1415 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
